# What operators should do next: make AI governable before it becomes operationally normal

*As of 2026-10-18. Part 3 of 3 in the Agentic GRC series.*

Critical-infrastructure operators should not wait for AI-specific law to become tidy before making AI governable.  

The practical move is to translate agentic AI into the evidence formats that risk, compliance and security teams already know: inventories, authorisations, accounts, access paths, communications, tests, vendor obligations and external-impact assessments. [03-c1] [03-c2] [03-c3] [03-c4] [03-c6]

That is my interpretation of the current signal from the evidence: the near-term governance problem is less “which grand AI framework will win” and more “can an auditor, regulator or board see what the AI can reach, what it can do, who approved it, and what it affects outside the fence?” [03-c2] [03-c3] [03-c4]

## Start with the AI you already have

Industrial Cyber reported Ampyx Cyber’s view that entities should know which products in their CIP-networked environments already have AI features, including features that vendors enabled after purchase. [03-c1]

That is a source claim, not direct operator testimony, but it is a useful control objective: inventory should cover embedded, bundled and later-enabled AI, not only tools bought under an “AI project” label. [03-c1]

For executives, the first question is therefore not whether the organisation has deployed an autonomous agent in operations; it is whether any product inside the governed environment has gained AI functionality that changes access, decision support, external communications or dependency on a vendor-managed service. [03-c1] [03-c2]

The second question is whether those features are visible in existing GRC systems. [03-c1] [03-c2]

If AI functionality sits in a CIP-networked product but does not appear in asset inventories, access reviews, change records, procurement files or vendor-risk reviews, then the organisation has created a governance gap before any spectacular AI failure occurs. [03-c1] [03-c2]

## Build an evidence file for every operational AI tool

Ampyx also says that, for each AI tool, entities should be able to show the CIP-004 authorisation, the account it runs under, the BCSI it can reach, and the communications it makes outside the ESP. [03-c2]

That sentence is the closest thing in this evidence set to an actionable checklist for AI in a regulated operational environment. [03-c2]

The file should answer four basic questions: who authorised the tool, what identity it uses, what sensitive information it can reach, and where it talks externally. [03-c2]

For agentic systems, I would add a fifth operational question to the same file: who can pause, revoke or narrow the tool’s authority when behaviour is uncertain. [03-c2]

That last point is an interpretation, but it follows from the same control logic: if authorisation and account identity matter, then revocation and constraint should be reviewable too. [03-c2]

This approach also reduces the temptation to treat AI governance as a separate policy exercise. [03-c2]

A board does not need a metaphysical definition of autonomy before it can require account ownership, least-privilege access, external-communications records and reviewable authorisation for AI-enabled tools in critical environments. [03-c2]

## Test the agent by reducing what it can use

IBM’s recent agent-engineering video is vendor content, so it should not be treated as independent evidence of what critical-infrastructure operators are doing. [03-c6]

Still, IBM’s technical claim is relevant to testing: agent controls may work by deliberately reducing what the agent can see or use. [03-c6]

IBM describes validation against something real, compaction of long context, curation of tools, and pruning of conflicting or superseded state as fixes for agent failure modes. [03-c6]

For a critical-infrastructure operator, the governance implication is straightforward: tests should not only ask whether the agent can complete a task, but whether it fails safely when context is stale, excessive, contradictory or tool access is broader than needed. [03-c6]

That turns “context engineering” from a developer technique into a control test that security, operations and compliance teams can observe. [03-c6]

The useful evidence is not a claim that these measures solve agent risk; it is that teams can design tests around validation, compaction, tool curation and pruning, then decide whether those tests are strong enough for operational use. [03-c6]

## Treat AI infrastructure as part of the governance perimeter

Utility Dive reported that proposed NERC standards for computational loads would apply to loads of at least 50 MW connected at voltage levels of at least 100 kV. [03-c3]

Utility Dive also reported that NERC’s board is expected to consider the standards in the fourth quarter, based on development timelines in the proposals. [03-c3]

Those are reported facts from the article, and they matter because AI governance is no longer only about software inside an operator’s environment. [03-c3]

Large AI data-centre interconnections can become reliability, modelling and communications issues for the power system itself. [03-c3]

Executives should therefore track whether these computational-load standards are approved and how their scope affects AI data-centre projects, customers, utilities and grid-planning assumptions. [03-c3]

CSIS’s podcast discussion adds a different governance signal: local backlash against data centres should not be dismissed simply as misinformation about water use. [03-c4]

In Jasmine Sun’s reporting discussed by CSIS, concerns also included electricity use, neighbourhood disruption, opaque deal processes, non-disclosure agreements and whether communities receive a fair bargain. [03-c4]

That is a source claim from a podcast discussion, not a formal regulatory finding, but it points to a real governance category: community legitimacy and electricity impacts belong in risk review, not only in communications planning. [03-c4]

For operators and AI customers, the question is whether data-centre siting, power demand and deal transparency are visible to the same leadership forums that review operational resilience and compliance exposure. [03-c4]

## Use the quantum precedent carefully

Singapore’s quantum-safe programme is not evidence about AI systems, and it should not be used to predict an AI regulatory timetable. [03-c5]

It is useful only as an analogy for how regulators can turn emerging-technology risk into practical obligations. [03-c5]

Industrial Cyber reported that Singapore’s advisory recommends quantum-safe migration plans by 2027 and migration by 2035 for organisations exposed to quantum-related cybersecurity risks. [03-c5]

The same report says the programme includes vendor and partner engagement, because readiness depends on theirs, and that pilot participants must submit reports of learnings and demonstrated impact. [03-c5]

The AI governance lesson is not “AI will follow the same dates”; it is that regulators can move from broad concern to exposure assessment, ownership, vendor engagement, deadlines and pilot evidence. [03-c5]

Operators that build those muscles now will be less exposed if AI-specific requirements later arrive in a similar form. [03-c5]

The main limitation is that this evidence set still contains little direct testimony from EU critical-infrastructure operators, and the community perspective appears mainly through one US-focused podcast discussion. [03-c4] [03-c5]

The remaining uncertainty is how quickly regulators will convert AI-specific operational risks into auditable requirements, and whether they will do so through AI law, sector rules, reliability standards or procurement pressure. [03-c3] [03-c5]

## What to watch

- Whether NERC’s computational-load standards are approved, and how the 50 MW and 100 kV scope affects AI data-centre interconnections. [03-c3]

- Whether vendors disclose AI features that are embedded, optional or enabled after procurement in CIP-networked products. [03-c1]

- Whether agent testing matures from performance demonstrations into evidence of validation, constrained context, curated tools and safe pruning of conflicting state. [03-c6]
